Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas · Conversation, family & daily routines

stupid adjective

also foolish, idiot, fool, dumb, dim, how stupid of me, stupidity, jerk, blockhead, dolt

classical

Cic. Sen. 67: quis est tam stultus …?
Ter. Eun. 2.2.1 (Lewis & Short)

stultus, stulta, stultum

adjective; comparative stultior; as a noun, stultus, a fool

stupid, foolish

The everyday word, in comedy and in Cicero alike, for a person, an act or an idea; stultē, stupidly; stultitia, stupidity.

Other words

  • stolidus, stolida, stolidum — dull, slow-witted, stupid

    also used · classical · Plaut. Aul. 3.2.1: quid, stolide, clāmās? (Lewis & Short); Liv. 22.28.9

    Stronger than stultus: dense, slow to take anything in; of things, inert. Common in comedy as an insult, and in Livy.

  • fatuus, fatua, fatuum — silly, idiotic

    also used · classical · Ter. Eun. 5.9.49: fatuus est, īnsulsus (Lewis & Short); Cic. Att. 6.6.3: puer

    Witless, a fool; of food, insipid (Mart. 13.13).

  • stupidus, stupida, stupidum — dazed, stunned; dull

    also used · classical · Cic. Par. 37: Echiōnis tabula tē stupidum dētinet (Lewis & Short); Cic. Fat. 10

    Not the everyday word for stupid, though English takes it from here: first struck dumb, rapt, gaping at a picture or a show, and only then dull or stupid (Zopyrus called Socrates stupidum et bardum, Cic. Fat. 10).

  • buccō, buccōnis m. — a babbler, blockhead

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Plaut. Bacch. 5.1.2 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 155

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut.)

    Lewis & Short: very rare. Traupman gives it for the colloquial “jerk”.

  • caudex (cōdex), caudicis m. — a blockhead (literally a tree stump)

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Ter. Heaut. 877 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 280

    (vōx cōmica: Ter.)

Examples

  • quis est tam stultus, quamvīs sit adulēscēns, cui sit explōrātum sē ad vesperum esse vīctūrum?

    who is so foolish, however young, as to be sure he will live till evening?Cic. Sen. 67

  • stultō intellegēns quid interest!

    what a difference between a man of sense and a fool!Ter. Eun. 2.2.1 (Lewis & Short)

  • Taciturnitās stultō hominī prō sapientiā est.

    for a fool, silence passes for wisdomPublil. Sent. T 16

See also silly, don’t be silly!, dull.
